summary: The posture is better than the architecture implies: every route in this set re-derives identity from the live session and most public endpoints already call the shared limiter, so no critical cross-tenant read or role escalation survived review. The one genuinely exploitable issue is competitive integrity: /api/parse-replay records any public Showdown battle between the two match participants as a game of that match, with no format, date, tournament or global replay-uniqueness binding, and the 24h auto-confirm turns a fabricated win into ratings, standings and bracket movement. Second tier is availability and broadcast integrity on the anonymous overlay surface, where the recap endpoint fans out ~40-50 uncached Postgres queries per request and does not verify that the season, tournament and round ids it was handed belong to each other. The rest are low-severity hardening items: a bearer-style Discord link-intent cookie that is not bound to the requesting session, two public read routes missing the limiter, an unbounded upstream fetch, a fail-open limiter on bootstrap, and a length-leaking secret compare. Fix the replay binding first; it is the only finding a free account can turn into a changed tournament result.

findings.title: Replay submission is not bound to the match: any past battle between the two participants counts as a game
findings.description: POST /api/parse-replay fetches any public Showdown replay (route.ts:33) and derives both PS usernames and the winner from the replay log itself (route.ts:34, 89). The only relationship asserted between the replay and the match is that each resolved username maps to match.player_1_id or match.player_2_id (route.ts:72-83). replay.format, the battle timestamp, the tournament/ruleset and the round are never compared, and recordGameResult re-checks only participant identity and match status (game-pipeline.ts:163-173). Duplicate protection loops over match.games only (game-pipeline.ts:100-109) and the schema deliberately leaves games.replay_url without a unique index (supabase/migrations/20261018130000_match_finalize_integrity.sql:12-15), so the same winning replay is reusable in a different match or a later round.
findings.path: authenticated participant -> POST /api/parse-replay { match_id, replay_url } -> fetchReplay(any public battle id) -> winner taken from the replay's |win| line -> recordGameResult with no format/date/uniqueness check -> games row + win count + pending_confirmation
findings.impact: A participant can bank a win in a scheduled or in-progress match using a friendly, a ladder game, an older tournament game, or a replay already used elsewhere. Because the winner id comes from the replay, reaching the Bo threshold moves the match to pending_confirmation with auto_confirm_at = now+24h (game-pipeline.ts:80-88); if the opponent does not actively dispute in that window, finalizeMatchCompletion propagates the fabricated result into aggregates, ratings, standings and the bracket. This is direct competitive-integrity manipulation with only a free account and one real replay where the caller beat the opponent.
findings.remediation: Before calling recordGameResult, require that the replay belongs to this match: compare replay.format against the tournament/round format mapping and reject a mismatch; optionally reject battles older than the match's scheduled_at or the round deadline. Store a normalized replay id on the game and enforce global uniqueness with a unique index (not just a scan of match.games). Keep any legitimate out-of-band import on the existing admin path.

verification.reason: Every decisive step checks out: POST /api/parse-replay is an ordinary participant route with no role gate, fetchReplay accepts any public Showdown replay id and returns its `format` but the route never reads it, the only replay-to-match binding is the participant identity check at route.ts:72-83, and recordGameResult validates actor/status and a match-scoped duplicate only — no format, timestamp, round or global replay-id comparison exists anywhere. The Bo threshold then sets pending_confirmation with a 24h timer, which the auto-confirm cron finalizes into ratings/bracket effects; the migration explicitly records that games.replay_url has no unique index, so the same replay can be reused in another match.

findings.title: Anonymous recap overlay endpoint is uncached and query-amplifying (per-match fan-out, no rate limit)
findings.description: GET /api/broadcast/recap/[sid] is public by design (route.ts:28) and validates only the UUID shape of its three ids (route.ts:49-56). composeWeeklyRecap then reads every match of the round (recap-engine.ts:71) and fans out two queries per completed match in a Promise.all (recap-engine.ts:76-82), plus getAggregates for leaders (recap-engine.ts:234), a paged getMatchesByTournament for standings movement and a round-wide usage fold (recap-engine.ts:297-329, 383-417). A 16-match round costs roughly 40-50 PostgREST round trips for one GET. The response sets no Cache-Control header (route.ts:97-100), unlike its siblings (standings/[sid]/route.ts:168-175, state/[mid]/route.ts:135-149), and the handler calls no rate limiter, although checkPublicRateLimit exists for exactly this class of route.
findings.path: anonymous request with three public UUIDs -> route handler -> composeWeeklyRecap -> 2N per-match queries + aggregates + paged tournament reads + usage fold -> service-role Postgres pool and Supabase egress
findings.impact: An anonymous caller can hold the shared service-role connection pool and egress at a large multiple of HTTP request rate, degrading match submission and draft routes during a live event. The legitimate OBS overlay pays the same cost on every poll, so the amplification is not hypothetical.
findings.remediation: Add the sibling cache header (public, s-maxage=30, stale-while-revalidate=60) so repeat overlay polls collapse at the edge, and gate the handler with checkPublicRateLimit (e.g. 30/min per IP). Optionally replace the per-match loops with one .in('match_id', ids) read each for stats and moments.

verification.reason: Every decisive fact holds: the handler is explicitly public with no auth or rate-limit import and returns NextResponse.json without a headers option (so no Cache-Control), while both cited sibling broadcast routes do set one; composeWeeklyRecap does read all round matches, fans out per-match stats and moments reads in Promise.all, and additionally calls getAggregates plus a paged getMatchesByTournament/getParticipants/getTournamentById for standings. The only imprecision is the per-match query count, which is higher than claimed (three, not two), strengthening the amplification rather than weakening it.
verification.corrections: Per-match cost is three PostgREST round trips, not two: getBattleStatsByMatch issues a `games` id select and then a `battle_stats` `.in('game_id', ids)` select (games.ts:526-539), and getMomentsByMatch issues one more (broadcast-moments.ts:23-28). A 16-match round is therefore roughly 55-60 round trips (1 round read + 3N + aggregates + paged tournament read + participants + tournament row + locale/season/tournament/round lookups), not 40-50 — the amplification is larger than stated. Also note computeStandingsMovement returns early when round_number <= 1, so the paged tournament read is skipped for a round-1 recap; the per-match fan-out is unaffected.

findings.title: parse-replay is an existence/identity oracle for PS usernames and, for non-participants, for match ids
findings.description: The handler loads the match before any participation check (route.ts:37-43), then resolves each PS username from the fetched replay and answers three distinguishable failures: 404 match_not_found, 400 name_mismatch when the username has no player row (route.ts:50-65), and 400 replay_player_not_in_match whose params embed the registered display name (route.ts:72-83). A caller who is not a participant therefore learns whether an arbitrary match UUID exists and, for any username appearing in a public replay, whether that Showdown account is linked and under which display name.
findings.path: authenticated player + any public replay containing the target username -> POST /api/parse-replay -> per-username getPlayerByPsUsername -> differential error code and params.player display name
findings.impact: Confirms PS-username-to-account bindings that other routes rely on to resolve identity, and discloses the internal display name attached to a linked account; caps at 20 requests/hour per account, which is enough for targeted enumeration.
findings.remediation: Load the match and enforce the participant check before resolving replay usernames, and return one generic code (e.g. replay_does_not_match_match) without embedding dbPlayer.name. For non-participants, do not distinguish match_not_found from the later failures.

verification.reason: The handler is mounted at /api/parse-replay (no middleware.ts exists; app-router file route, no rewrites in next.config.mjs), requires any signed-in player, then calls getMatchById(body.match_id) and returns 404 match_not_found before any participation check. The only participation guard in the whole flow lives downstream in recordGameResult (game-pipeline.ts:163-169), after both the per-username lookup and the mismatched-participant response have already been returned, and getPlayerByPsUsername selects '*', so dbPlayer.name is real data embedded in params.player. Tests in __tests__/route.test.ts:186-222 confirm the three responses are distinguishable, so the differential oracle exists exactly as described.

evidence.quote:
expect(body.code).toBe('replay_player_not_in_match');
    expect(body.params).toEqual({ username: 'alice_ps', player: 'Stranger' });

verification.corrections: Two imprecisions worth fixing in the write-up. (1) The display-name disclosure comes only from the 'replay_player_not_in_match' branch (params.player = dbPlayer.name, route.ts:77); 'name_mismatch' carries just params.username plus the ps_usernames list, so it proves only that no players row matches that PS name. (2) The attacker cannot inject arbitrary usernames: parseReplaySchema does not validate replay_url as a URL, but fetchReplay rewrites it and fetches from replay.pokemonshowdown.com only (src/lib/pkmn/replay.ts:30-35), so the probed usernames must appear in a real public PS replay — which is public data, so the precondition holds, but brute-forcing arbitrary PS names requires a replay containing each one (own battles against the target, or the target's existing public replays). Also note the leak is per-request first-failure only (the loop returns on the first unresolved or non-participant username), and matches are already listed on public league/match pages, so the match-id existence signal is the weaker half of the finding; the PS-username-to-display-name binding is the real disclosure.

findings.title: Discord link intent is an unbound bearer cookie (no session binding, no __Host- prefix)
findings.description: The link flow signs only the player id plus an expiry (crypto.ts:27-31) and stores it in __poketools_link_discord with path=/, no Domain and no __Host- prefix (link-discord/route.ts:42-48). On any later Discord sign-in the callback reads whatever token is in the cookie, verifies the HMAC and links the just-authenticated Discord identity to that player id (auth.ts:194-219); nothing checks that the presenter is still the identity that requested the link, and nothing binds the token to the issuing session. Because the cookie name is not host-locked, a sibling subdomain can plant a token (minted for free from the attacker's own account) scoped to the registrable domain, and the app cannot distinguish it from its own.
findings.path: attacker mints a valid intent for their own player (POST /api/account/link-discord) -> plants __poketools_link_discord on the parent domain from a sibling subdomain or XSS -> victim completes Discord sign-in within 10 minutes -> linkDiscordToPlayer(attacker player, victim discord id)
findings.impact: Account takeover / link pre-hijacking: the victim's Discord identity is attached to a player row the attacker controls, and the attacker retains access through Discord afterwards. Requires subdomain control (or script execution on any *.<production-domain> origin) plus a sign-in inside the 10-minute TTL, which is why it is scored low, not critical.
findings.remediation: Rename to __Host-poketools_link_discord so the browser rejects any Domain attribute, and bind the intent to its origin: sign a nonce that is also stored server-side against the requesting auth_user_id and deleted on consumption, or verify that the current session identity matches the one that requested the link.

verification.reason: Every decisive fact checks out: the intent token is HMAC over only player id + expiry, is stored in a cookie literally named __poketools_link_discord with path=/ and no Domain/__Host- prefix, and the Discord signIn callback verifies only the HMAC and then calls linkDiscordToPlayer for the payload's player id without ever consulting the current session identity — the sole guard is that the target row has no discord_id yet. The route is a mounted App Router handler (POST, requirePlayer) that mints exactly such a token for any authenticated player with no linked Discord, so an attacker can obtain a valid intent and a victim Discord sign-in within the TTL will be attached to that player row.

verification.corrections: Direction/imprecision: this is pre-hijacking, not takeover of a victim's existing account. The link only fires when the presented Discord id is not already attached to any player (auth.ts:213-216) and only when the attacker's player row has no discord_id (players.ts:165), so the outcome is the victim's Discord identity landing on the attacker's player row — the victim's existing accounts remain untouched, and the victim would have to complete Discord sign-in themselves for the attacker to gain anything. The sibling-subdomain planting step is standard browser cookie-tossing (a child origin can set a Domain=<parent> cookie), which the code cannot prevent given the name lacks the __Host- prefix; the claim itself conditions on subdomain control or script execution, consistent with the low score and with DNS/TLS config being out of scope.

findings.title: Recap endpoint never checks that tournament_id and round_id belong to the season in the path
findings.description: The handler validates UUID shape (route.ts:49-56) and that each row exists (route.ts:59-82), but never asserts tournament.season_id === sid or round.tournament_id === tournament.id. composeWeeklyRecap then mixes sources: league_label from season.name, tournament and round labels from the caller-supplied rows (route.ts:86-94), and match/stat data from getMatchesByRound(roundId), which is itself not season-scoped (matches.ts:159-167).
findings.path: anonymous query string -> three independent row lookups -> no relationship check -> recap payload mixing league A branding with league B matches and leaders
findings.impact: Broadcast display integrity: an overlay URL can be made to show one league's name and branding over another league's results and stat leaders, and a caster cannot tell the payload is inconsistent. No private rows are exposed, since the underlying match and stat data is already public.
findings.remediation: After the three lookups, reject with the existing 404 codes unless tournament.season_id === sid and round.tournament_id === tournament.id. Both fields are already on the rows the handler reads.

findings.title: Public solo overlay serves any solo cast session by id, including unpublished draft sessions and the owner's player UUID
findings.description: The route is public by design (route.ts:82) and its only gate is session.mode !== 'solo' (route.ts:91). getCastSessionById loads the row with select('*') (cast-sessions.ts:93-97); there is no owner check, no status check and no publication check, so a session still in draft is served identically to a live one. buildPublicState returns both species lists (route.ts:43-48), the stored opponent name (route.ts:42), tracker slots and W/L (route.ts:49-77), and player1_id, which falls back to session.owner_id, a player UUID (solo-defaults.ts:35, surfaced at route.ts:40).
findings.path: anonymous GET with a known cast-session UUID -> getCastSessionById (select *) -> mode-only check -> buildPublicState -> unpublished species lists, per-game winners, opponent name and owner player id
findings.impact: Anyone holding one session UUID (it is embedded in OBS overlay URLs, stream layouts and studio links) can read team composition for a session prepared but not yet shown, plus the owner's player UUID for chaining into player-scoped routes. The UUID is 128-bit and not enumerable, so this is a link-disclosure issue rather than a bulk leak.
findings.remediation: Gate on session.status !== 'draft' so only live/ended sessions are public, and return an opaque public id (or omit the field) instead of the owner's player UUID. An optional signed per-session overlay token would remove the guess-the-UUID property entirely.

verification.reason: Every decisive fact checks out: the handler at src/app/api/broadcast/solo/[sessionId]/route.ts:83-105 performs no auth and its sole gate is session.mode !== 'solo' (line 91), while getCastSessionById (src/lib/supabase/queries/cast-sessions.ts:92-104) filters only on id after select('*'), so status/owner are never consulted; the column defaults to 'draft' (supabase/migrations/20260608100000_baseline_professional_schema.sql:942) and the create path never overrides it, so freshly created solo sessions are readable by anyone with the id. buildPublicState then returns both species lists, stored player2_name, tracker slots plus computed wins/losses, and a player UUID in player1_id (solo-defaults.ts:35 falls back to owner_id, which is an FK to public.players(id)), and there is no middleware.ts or config-level gate to intercept the route.

findings.title: League admin page admits any resource admin, not an admin of the requested league
findings.description: The page gates only on access?.isAnyAdmin (page.tsx:79), which getLiveAccess derives from resource_admins(count) > 0 for any resource (helpers.ts:134). It then renders the full admin shell for the requested season: status control, description editor, participant/group/core managers, phase timeline and archive control (page.tsx:113-130). The repo's own per-match gate is stricter, calling isResourceAdminFor(player, 'tournament', id) after the isAnyAdmin test (match-access.tsx:24-29).
findings.path: resource admin of league A -> GET /admin/leagues/<league B id> -> isAnyAdmin passes -> full admin shell rendered for league B
findings.impact: A resource admin of one league can open another league's admin shell and read its configuration, and operate controls that appear functional but are refused by the APIs. No write succeeds today because the routes re-check the resource, but the page-level gate is a latent cross-tenant hole for any future control that trusts it.
findings.remediation: Mirror canAdministerMatch: after the isAnyAdmin test, return the guard/denied component unless access.isSiteAdmin or isResourceAdminFor(access.player.playerId, 'season', id) is true, reusing the memoised helper so the layout read is shared.

verification.reason: Every decisive fact checks out: the page's only gate is `if (!access?.isAnyAdmin)` after loading the league row, `AdminGuard` itself only re-tests `isAnyAdmin`, and `isAnyAdmin` is true for a player holding any `resource_admins` row (`resource_admin_count > 0`) regardless of which resource it names — so a season/tournament admin of league A can render league B's admin shell. No per-resource check exists anywhere on this route or in its panels, while the sibling per-match gate does add one after the same `isAnyAdmin` test; the write APIs are separately re-guarded, so the impact is read/latent as the claim describes.

findings.title: Image proxy validates the requested URL but fetches with redirects followed and port ignored
findings.description: The allowlist test compares parsed.hostname and parsed.pathname against two literal host/path pairs (route.ts:52-54), but the fetch at route.ts:63 uses the raw string with undici's default redirect:'follow', so any 3xx from an allowlisted host is followed to a host that was never checked. Comparing hostname also ignores the port, so https://play.pokemonshowdown.com:<any-port>/sprites/... passes and is contacted. The upstream Content-Type is then echoed verbatim under an image/ prefix test (route.ts:72-73, 87) with a 7-day public cache.
findings.path: anonymous GET /api/proxy-image?url=... -> hostname+path allowlist (no port, no redirect handling) -> fetch follows 3xx -> bytes and Content-Type reflected from the final origin
findings.impact: A residual outbound-fetch primitive and an origin for reflected content: if any allowlisted /sprites/ path ever redirects (CDN move, open-redirect parameter), an anonymous caller can make the function fetch an arbitrary URL and receive the body, cached at the edge for a week. No redirect is demonstrated on either host in this snapshot, which is why this is defense-in-depth rather than a live SSRF.
findings.remediation: Fetch with redirect: 'manual' and return 502 on any 3xx (or re-parse response.url and re-run the same host+path check before reading the body); compare parsed.host rather than parsed.hostname so a non-default port fails; narrow the accepted types to png/gif/jpeg/webp instead of the image/ prefix, and add Content-Disposition: inline plus a per-route CSP sandbox.

verification.reason: Every cited element exists exactly as described: the allowlist compares parsed.hostname and pathname only (no parsed.port check), the fetch passes only a timeout signal so the runtime's default redirect:'follow' applies, and the final response's Content-Type is echoed verbatim under an 'image/' startsWith test with s-maxage=604800. The route is publicly mounted at /api/proxy-image (src/app/api/proxy-image/route.ts) with only a 60/min rate limit, so the residual primitive is real; the finding correctly self-limits to defense-in-depth since no redirect on the two allowlisted hosts is demonstrated.

verification.corrections: Two precision notes, neither changing the verdict: (1) the fetched bytes are only returned if the FINAL response after redirects is both ok (2xx) and image/*-typed, since response.ok and the Content-Type check are evaluated on the post-redirect response — a 3xx alone yields no body; the exposure is the followed request plus whatever image-typed body the redirect target returns. (2) The check is pathPrefix startsWith on the normalized URL pathname, so query strings are ignored by the allowlist; this is what makes an open-redirect parameter on an allowlisted /sprites/ URL the plausible trigger, as the finding already states.

findings.title: Bootstrap secret is guarded by a fail-open limiter and failures are not audited
findings.description: The only credential for promoting the first admin is a shared BOOTSTRAP_SECRET compared in constant time (route.ts:79, crypto.ts:16-20). The rate gate at route.ts:57 passes no failMode, so the default 'open' applies and any RPC error, timeout or missing row returns allowed:true (rate-limit.ts:134-138); getClientIp collapses to a shared 'unknown' identity when headers are absent (rate-limit.ts:296-298). Failed comparisons produce no log line and no audit row, since logAuditEvent only fires on success (route.ts:137).
findings.path: anonymous POST /api/bootstrap -> limiter (fails open) -> secretsEqual against a static env secret -> first successful guess promotes the caller's own signed-in player to is_admin
findings.impact: Whoever guesses or leaks the secret during the pre-first-admin window becomes site admin with service-role-equivalent authority through the routes, and the limiter is the only volume control. The window closes permanently once any admin exists (route.ts:60-76), so exposure is limited to a fresh install or a misconfigured one.
findings.remediation: Pass failMode:'closed' at route.ts:57 (this is the abuse-worse-than-outage case the limiter documents), log and count failed comparisons without the submitted value, and enforce a minimum secret length/entropy in requireEnv so a short secret cannot be configured.

verification.reason: Every decisive fact checks out in the source. findings.title: Cron routes use a length-short-circuiting compare for CRON_SECRET
findings.description: All four cron handlers compare the bearer token with timingSafeCompare, which returns false before timingSafeEqual when the buffer lengths differ (crypto.ts:6). Requests with a token of the wrong length therefore short-circuit earlier than one of the correct length, leaking the expected secret's length. crypto.ts already exports the length-independent secretsEqual used by the bootstrap route, so this is a divergence from a known invariant rather than a missing capability.
findings.path: anonymous Authorization header -> authHeader.slice(7) -> timingSafeCompare(provided, CRON_SECRET) -> early return on length mismatch
findings.impact: A remote observer could in principle learn CRON_SECRET's length and narrow a brute force. Measuring a few microseconds of difference against a serverless function is practically infeasible, and no content is disclosed.
findings.remediation: Replace timingSafeCompare with secretsEqual in all four cron routes; the call signature is identical.

dismissed.title: parse-replay discloses existence of arbitrary match ids to non-participants
dismissed.reason: Match pages and tournament pages already publish match ids and participants, so the 404-vs-400 distinction adds no confidentiality. Only the PS-username-to-registered-account binding survives, which is retained in F3.

dismissed.title: proxy-image SSRF reaching link-local/metadata addresses
dismissed.reason: As stated this is not reachable in the snapshot: the protocol is forced to https, the host is compared against two literal entries, and neither allowlisted host was shown to redirect from a /sprites/ path. The metadata-read impact is speculative; the concrete, verifiable defects (redirect handling and port being ignored) are kept in F8 as hardening.

dismissed.title: Solo overlay player UUID enables chaining into other player-scoped routes
dismissed.reason: No route in this finding set authorizes on a bare player UUID - the player-scoped writes reviewed here all require the live session identity. The owner UUID is noted inside F6 but no chain is claimed.
